::: {.gw-box}
**Today's idea:** Week 9 colored regions someone else had already drawn. This
week the data is **points**, and nobody has drawn anything. Everything on the
map — the groups, the boundaries, the density — is something you computed, and
every one of those computations took a parameter.
:::

Running example: **2,264 Tesla Supercharger sites** in the United States, with
coordinates, stall counts and opening dates.

# Points are not polygons {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## The data has no shape of its own {.smaller}

A choropleth starts with regions. Someone drew the state boundaries, the census
decided which tract is which, and your job was to pick a color.

A set of points has none of that. 2,264 latitude and longitude pairs do not
come divided into anything. If you want regions, groups or neighborhoods, you
have to **make them**, and that is a modeling decision rather than a
cartographic one.

::: {#a2bbc1d0 .cell execution_count=1}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
2264 sites in the file, 2254 in the contiguous states
25,451 charging stalls
opened between 2012-11-19 and 2023-06-03
```
:::
:::


## The first problem: overplotting {.smaller}

::: {#6d7f4548 .cell execution_count=2}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week10_map_visualization_ii_files/figure-revealjs/cell-3-output-1.png){width=1142 height=346 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


On the left, the northeast is a solid shape. Ten sites and a hundred sites look
exactly the same once the dots overlap, so the densest part of the map — the
part you most want to read — is the part carrying the least information.

**A choropleth cannot do this.** Each region gets one patch of color, however
many observations went into it.

## What transparency buys, and what it does not

Making the dots see-through is the cheapest fix and it is a real improvement:
stacking now shows as darkness, so you can tell dense from sparse.

It still cannot tell you **how many**. There is no legend you could add, because
the mapping from "how dark" to "how many" depends on the dot size, the opacity
and the zoom, all at once.

If the answer needs a number, the dots have to be counted. That is the next
section.

# Density {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Counting points into a grid {.smaller}

Lay a grid over the map, count how many points fall in each cell, color the
cells. The dots become a surface you can put a legend on.

::: {#a7f5e371 .cell execution_count=3}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week10_map_visualization_ii_files/figure-revealjs/cell-4-output-1.png){width=1334 height=323 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


## The resolution is the story {.smaller}

Read the three panels as three different claims:

- **Coarse** says the sites are on the coasts. True, and it hides everything
  else.
- **Medium** says there are distinct metropolitan concentrations.
- **Fine** says there are individual cities, and starts to look like the dot
  map again because most cells now hold one point.

Nothing about the data changed. This is the same situation as Week 9's class
breaks: **the parameter is part of the result**, so it belongs in the caption.
A density map without its resolution stated cannot be reproduced.

A density surface also invents something the data does not contain — a value
*between* the points, where nothing was observed. That is usually what you
want, and it is worth knowing you asked for it.

# Distance {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Degrees are not a distance {.smaller}

Week 9 made this point about area. It returns here, and it is sharper, because
distance is the whole subject.

::: {#406e4169 .cell execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
at 26N, one degree of longitude =  100.1 km
at 38N, one degree of longitude =   87.7 km
at 48N, one degree of longitude =   74.5 km
at 61N, one degree of longitude =   54.0 km

at every latitude, one degree of latitude = ~111.0 km
```
:::
:::


A degree of latitude is a fixed distance. A degree of longitude is not — it
shrinks toward the poles, because the lines of longitude meet there. So
`sqrt(dlat**2 + dlon**2)`, the formula everyone reaches for first, is measuring
in a unit that changes as you move north.

## Haversine {.smaller}

The **haversine** formula gives the distance between two points along the
surface of a sphere. It is the right tool for latitude and longitude, and it is
built into the libraries you already have:

```python
from sklearn.neighbors import BallTree

tree = BallTree(np.radians(coords), metric="haversine")   # radians, not degrees
distances, indices = tree.query(np.radians(coords), k=2)  # k=2: itself, then the nearest
km = distances[:, 1] * 6371.0088                          # Earth's radius in km
```

Two details that cause silent wrong answers:

- it wants **radians**, and will happily accept degrees and return nonsense
- the result is an **angle**, so multiply by the Earth's radius to get distance

## How far is the nearest one? {.smaller}

This is a question a choropleth cannot answer. A map of chargers-per-state
tells you nothing about the drive.

::: {#a6ad05ef .cell execution_count=5}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week10_map_visualization_ii_files/figure-revealjs/cell-6-output-1.png){width=853 height=267 fig-align='center'}
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
median 7.9 km | mean 19.2 km | 90th percentile 55.2 km
```
:::
:::


The mean is more than twice the median, which is the histogram's long right tail
showing up as a number. **Report the median.**

## The far end of that column {.smaller}

::: {#cb333eea .cell execution_count=6}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
            name state  nearest_km
       Hines, OR    OR       168.0
       Lamar, CO    CO       158.0
       Minot, ND    ND       158.0
    Bismarck, ND    ND       151.0
Rock Springs, WY    WY       148.0
```
:::
:::


Real answers about coverage, from the points alone. Hines, Oregon is 168 km
from its nearest neighbor — that is the gap, and no choropleth of Oregon would
have shown it.

## And the near end {.smaller}

::: {#21591308 .cell execution_count=7}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
                                    name state  nearest_km
St. George - Convention Center Drive, UT    UT       0.036
 St. George - S Convention Center Dr, UT    UT       0.036
                   Baker (Expansion), CA    CA       0.037
                               Baker, CA    CA       0.037
                   Nephi - S Main St, UT    UT       0.047
                               Nephi, UT    UT       0.047
```
:::
:::


**Thirty-six metres.** Read the names: `Baker, CA` and `Baker (Expansion), CA`.
`St. George - Convention Center Drive` and `St. George - S Convention Center Dr`.

These are the same place, entered twice. A query written to answer a coverage
question has found a **data quality problem** instead — and it was invisible in
every map so far, because at national zoom the two dots are one dot.

Decide what to do about them before you count anything.

# Finding groups {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## DBSCAN {.smaller}

Points that sit close together in dense bunches get grouped; everything else is
labeled **noise**. Unlike k-means it is not told how many groups to find, and
it is not required to put every point in one.

It takes two numbers:

- **`eps`** — how far apart still counts as "close"
- **`min_samples`** — how many neighbors within `eps` a point needs before it
  can anchor a group

That is the whole algorithm. Both numbers are yours to choose, and the answer
changes when they do.

## The mistake that makes it wrong {.smaller}

The obvious call is `DBSCAN(eps=0.45)` on a table of latitude and longitude,
with `eps` worked out as 50 km divided by 111 km per degree.

It runs. It returns clusters. It is wrong, for the reason two slides back: that
`eps` means 50 km north-south and something else east-west, varying with
latitude.

::: {#af5593f9 .cell execution_count=8}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
haversine on radians    50 clusters,  607 points left as noise
euclidean on degrees    48 clusters,  706 points left as noise
```
:::
:::


## How much does it cost? {.smaller}

Cluster numbers are handed out in the order DBSCAN finds them, so comparing
"cluster 7" across two runs is meaningless. Two things do survive relabeling:

::: {#77e6b1a7 .cell execution_count=9}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
adjusted Rand index: 0.864   (1.0 would be the same grouping)

points whose noise status differs: 99 of 2254
  clustered by haversine, called noise by euclidean: 99
  the reverse:                                       0

  south of 34N    585 sites, differs for  3.4%
  34 to 42N      1288 sites, differs for  4.0%
  north of 42N    381 sites, differs for  7.1%
```
:::
:::


**Every disagreement runs the same way**, and the error grows with latitude.
Nothing raises an exception. The northern states simply end up with fewer
clusters than they should have.

## Reading the result {.smaller}

::: {#76f81b85 .cell execution_count=10}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
50 clusters, 607 points as noise. The six largest:
         sites  stalls   lat    lon
cluster                            
0          424    3989  40.5  -74.4
10         245    4284  34.0 -118.1
5          220    3084  37.8 -121.6
4          132    1403  27.5  -81.2
9           58     646  42.0  -87.7
12          47     503  35.6  -79.6
```
:::
:::


## Check the groups are real {.smaller}

DBSCAN was given coordinates and nothing else. No city names, no state
boundaries, no population.

Read the centroids anyway:

- **40.5N, −74.4W** — New York and northern New Jersey
- **34.0N, −118.1W** — Los Angeles
- **37.8N, −121.6W** — the Bay Area
- **27.5N, −81.2W** — central Florida

It recovered the metropolitan areas from the dots. That agreement is your
evidence the parameters were sensible — and it is the check to run before
believing any clustering, because the algorithm will return groups whether or
not there are any.

## Noise is not failure {.smaller}

::: {#1ee5bd67 .cell execution_count=11}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![](week10_map_visualization_ii_files/figure-revealjs/cell-12-output-1.png){width=730 height=432 fig-align='center'}
:::
:::


For a charging network the grey points may be the **most** interesting
category: the lone stations on long highways, built so the gap is covered
rather than because demand was dense.

# Putting it in front of someone {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Performance is a design choice {.smaller}

Interactive maps send every feature to the browser. How you draw 2,254 points
changes the page by a factor of nearly four:

::: {#d621ce77 .cell execution_count=12}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
the same 2,254 points, four ways of drawing them in folium:
  one CircleMarker per point : 1,481 KB
  MarkerCluster              :   474 KB
  one Marker per point       :   449 KB
  a single GeoJson layer     :   401 KB
```
:::
:::


`CircleMarker` writes a separate JavaScript object per point; a `GeoJson` layer
writes one object holding all of them. The map looks nearly identical.

At this size it is a slow page. At ten times this size it is a page that does
not load, and the usual answer is to stop sending raw points — cluster them,
aggregate them to a grid, or send only what is in view.

## Restraint {.smaller}

Every control you add costs the reader something. The standard ordering, from
Shneiderman, is **overview first, zoom and filter, details on demand** — give
the whole picture, let them narrow it, and keep the specifics for when they
ask.

Applied here: show the density surface first, let them filter by state or by
opening year, and put the site name and stall count in a tooltip rather than
on the map.

A map with every layer switched on, every point labeled and a popup on
everything is not a more informative map. It is a map nobody reads.

## Discussion {.gw-discussion}

**1.** Your clustering returns 50 groups. Your colleague runs the same code and
gets 48. Neither of you changed the data. What do you need to tell each other
before you can say which is right — and is "which is right" even the question?

**2.** You find two sites 36 metres apart. One is named "Expansion". Do you
merge them, drop one, or keep both — and what does each choice do to a map of
coverage?
